turns.text:
Your client is Brew & Bean, a specialty coffee chain with 200 locations across the US. Over the past two years, their net profit margin has declined from 24% to 6%, even though revenues have grown 15% over the same period. The CEO has hired us to identify the root cause of this profit decline and recommend how to reverse it. How would you approach this problem?

Whenever you're ready, walk me through your thinking.

Happy to dive in. So just to play back: 200 locations, net margin down from 24% to 6% over two years, revenue up 15%. So profit dollars have fallen hard even with growth — margin compression, not a demand problem.

My structure would be profit equals revenue minus cost, and I'd break each side down. On revenue: price per unit, volume, and mix across locations and product lines — is the 15% coming from new stores or same-store growth? On cost: fixed versus variable, so rent and leases, labor, cost of goods like beans and milk, and then corporate overhead.

Given revenue is up but margin is down, my hypothesis is costs are growing faster than revenue. So I'd start on the cost side.

Could I get the cost structure — ideally the major cost lines as a percent of revenue, for both the start and end of the two-year period?

A revenue-and-cost split. I'll come back to the cost structure as a percent of revenue shortly. Before we get into data: you're starting on the cost side. Is your structure MECE, what might it be missing, and why does cost come first rather than revenue?

I think it's broadly MECE on the arithmetic — revenue minus cost covers everything, and within cost, fixed versus variable doesn't overlap. Where it's probably not clean is that I lumped "mix" under revenue when mix also drives cost: a shift toward, say, food items changes COGS, not just price.

What I'm missing: I didn't say anything about non-operating items. Net margin, not operating margin, so interest expense, depreciation from a buildout, or taxes could be doing the damage and I'd never find it in store-level costs. I should also separate new stores from mature stores — if they opened aggressively, new units carry fixed costs before they ramp, and that drags blended margin even if nothing is wrong.

Cost first is really just a hypothesis from the prompt: revenue grew 15% while margin fell 18 points. If price and volume are both intact, the leak is more likely on cost. But I'd want to confirm revenue quality before committing — if the 15% is all new stores and same-store sales are falling, that changes the story.
Understood. Here's an exhibit: Brew & Bean Cost Structure Over Time. With those figures in hand, where do you see the margin compression coming from, and what would you dig into next?

Okay, this is clean — labor is flat at 22 all three years, overhead barely moves 12 to 13 to 14, so that's two points over two years. COGS goes 42 to 50 to 58. That's a 16-point swing, and profit falls exactly 18 points, so COGS is essentially the whole story.

Let me size it. If I take the current COGS rate of 58% and apply it to the base-year revenue, versus the 42% they used to run at, that's a 16-point gap on the original revenue base — so on every $100 of two-years-ago revenue, they're now burning $16 more on cost of goods. Across 200 stores that's the bleed.

And notice COGS rose 8 points each year, very linear — that smells like an input cost, not a one-time event. Green coffee and dairy both ran up over that period.

Do we have menu price history? If prices never moved while bean costs climbed, that's the mechanism.

A COGS-first read. Menu prices have held flat over the past two years. You said green coffee and dairy both ran up. Without assuming either, which input is driving the COGS increase, and what would you want to see to tell them apart?

Fair — I shouldn't have named a culprit without the data. What I can say is COGS is a basket: beans, dairy, cups and lids, food, syrups. The increase could be unit price on one input, a volume shift toward a more expensive input, or a mix shift toward low-margin items like food and cold drinks, which carry more milk and packaging per ticket.

To tell them apart I'd want COGS broken into its components as a percent of revenue across the three years, plus unit costs — dollars per pound of green coffee, dollars per gallon of milk — so I can separate price-per-unit from quantity used.

One read I'd test from the exhibit: overhead moved 12 to 14, so 2 points of the 16. If that same 2-point share applies inside COGS, roughly 2 of the 16 points is packaging and non-input drag, leaving about 14 points sitting in beans and dairy. That'd tell me this is concentrated in one or two inputs, not spread thin.

Understood. Coffee beans made up 25% of COGS two years ago. Over the past two years, raw coffee bean costs have risen 40%. Dairy, packaging, and food — the other input costs — are up 37.5% over the past two years. On that two-of-sixteen split: you carried the overhead share over into COGS. Walk me through why overhead's movement tells you anything about packaging inside COGS. Then, with these figures, which input is driving the increase?

You're right to push — that was a stretch. Overhead is rent, corporate, admin; packaging sits in COGS. There's no reason one line's drift tells me anything about a component of another. I was pattern-matching on the number 2 because it was convenient. Scratch it.

Let me use the actual figures. Beans are 25% of COGS, and COGS is currently 58 points of revenue, so beans are 0.25 × 58 = 14.5 points. The other inputs are the remaining 43.5 points. Now apply the growth: beans up 40%, so 14.5 × 0.40 = 5.8 points of increase. Everything else up 37.5%, but that's spread across dairy, packaging, and food — three separate inputs, so call it roughly 2 points each.

So beans at 5.8 points is the single largest contributor by a wide margin, more than double any other line, and it has the steepest growth rate at 40%. Coffee beans are driving the COGS increase. That's the one to attack.
Understood. What would you look at next, and why?

Two things, in order.

First, I'd size what fixing beans buys us. Beans are 5.8 points of the 16-point COGS increase. If we could hold bean costs at the old level, margin goes from 6% to roughly 11.8% — so call it 12%. That's meaningful but it doesn't get us back to 24, which tells me beans are the driver but not the whole fix, and I'd want to be honest with the CEO about that gap.

Second, procurement. I'd look at how they buy green coffee — spot versus forward contracts, how many suppliers, contract length. A 40% run-up over two years with flat menu prices suggests they're exposed to spot and never hedged.

Then the pricing side, since prices have been flat for two years. I'd want elasticity — how much can a specialty chain pass through before volume moves?

Do we have transaction volume by store over the period? Want to be sure same-store traffic is steady before I recommend a price increase.

Mm-hm. At $6.80, the average transaction is about 10% higher than the $6.20 of two years ago, because customers are buying more items per visit. You took beans as 25% of the 58 points of COGS. Which year does that 25% refer to, and what was COGS then?

Sure. Beans were 25% of COGS. I took the current COGS line, 58 points of revenue, and multiplied: 0.25 × 58 = 14.5 points of revenue sitting in beans today. Then beans rose 40% over the two years, so the increase is 14.5 × 0.40 = 5.8 points of revenue.

And the transaction figure actually reinforces the pricing story. Average ticket is $6.80 now versus $6.20 two years ago — so a cup of coffee effectively goes for $6.80. If beans run at 14.5% of revenue, that's about $0.99 of bean cost in that $6.80 cup, up from roughly $0.71 before the run-up. So customers are absorbing nothing, because menu prices held flat — the whole $0.28 landed on us.

A 5% price increase on $6.80 is about $0.34, which more than covers the bean inflation per cup. That's a clean, small ask of the customer.
